draft.title: The anti-war movement
card: As the Vietnam War went on, more Australians came to oppose it. Many objected to conscription, because men aged 20 were sent to fight but could not vote for the government that sent them.
Opponents included students, unions, church groups and families of soldiers. Some conscripts refused to register or serve, and some people helped them.

In 1970 the Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam held mass marches in Australian cities. Moratorium means a pause, and the marchers called for a pause in normal life to protest. Huge crowds took part, including in Melbourne.
Public opinion shifted against the war. Australia began withdrawing troops in 1970, and the last combat troops came home in the early 1970s.
draft.remember: Opposition grew from objections to conscription into mass marches, and combat troops were later withdrawn.

a.q: What was the Moratorium movement in 1970?
opts: Mass marches in cities calling for an end to the war
A government plan to bring conscripts home early
A vote to decide whether conscription should continue
A strike by soldiers who refused to fight in Vietnam
a.why: The Moratorium was a series of large public marches against Australia's part in the war. It was a protest by citizens, not a government plan or a vote. The soldiers did not strike.
a.clue: Think of what crowds did in city streets.

b.q: Which statement best matches the history of the protests and Australia's combat role?
opts: Protests grew with public opinion, and troops came home
Troops came home first, and then the marches began
The 1970 marches ended the war the same year
Protests were ignored and no troops came home until 1975
b.why: Opposition grew and opinion turned against the war, and combat troops were withdrawn from 1970 to the early 1970s. The third option is tempting, but the marches did not end the war on their own. Withdrawal began in 1970 and was not finished that year.
b.clue: The marches began in 1970, and the last combat troops left a little later.

a.best: Mass marches in cities calling for an end to the war

b.best: Protests grew with public opinion, and troops came home

problems.detail: The clue 'Think of what crowds did in city streets' points straight at the only option about crowds marching in cities, so it gives the answer away.
The clue says the marches began in 1970 and the troops left later, which rules out the distractors ('Troops came home first', 'ended the war the same year') and gives the answer away.

Why (b) calls 'the third option' the marches-ended-the-war distractor. The options are shuffled, and in this order the third option is 'Troops came home first, and then the marches began', so the reference is wrong and confusing.

'Some conscripts refused to register' is slightly inaccurate. Men who refused to register had not yet been conscripted. 'Some young men refused to register, and some conscripts refused to serve' would be clearer.

check.summary: The facts check out and each question has one clear right answer. Both clues give the answer away, Why (b) points to the 'third option' when the options are shuffled, and the card wrongly calls men who would not register 'conscripts'.
